sentences.text: Adult Daspletosaurus measured between 8.5 and 9 meters long and weighed 2 to 3 metric tons.
This massive predator stood 2.2 meters tall at the hip and walked on two thick hindlimbs ending in four-toed feet.
The first digit of its foot did not touch the ground during movement.
Its teeth in the premaxilla featured a D-shaped cross-section, a trait of heterodonty common in tyrannosaurids.
Comparisons of tooth wear suggest the animal had lips that protected its teeth from external influences.
Large flat scales likely covered its snout to protect it during prey capture and fights with other individuals.
One large specimen suggests the animal could reach lengths over 9 meters, potentially up to 11 meters and 4 to 5 metric tons in weight.
A potential D. torosus specimen nicknamed "Pete III" indicates the genus could reach nearly 11 meters in length and weigh 5 tons.
Evidence of cannibalism in Daspletosaurus was published in 2015.
A full-grown fossil from the Dinosaur Park Formation shows bite marks on its skull.
The genus Daspletosaurus was described by Dale Russell in 1970.
The name Daspletosaurus comes from Greek meaning "terrible lizard," and the type species D. torosus means "muscular" in Latin.
The type specimen of Daspletosaurus torosus was discovered in 1921 near Steveville, Alberta, by Charles Mortram Sternberg.
Barnum Brown collected a specimen in 1913 that was designated as the paratype of Daspletosaurus torosus.
Fossils of the type species Daspletosaurus torosus have been found in Alberta.
Daspletosaurus likely preyed on large dinosaurs such as the ceratopsid Centrosaurus and the hadrosaur Hypacrosaurus.
The skull was built to absorb the impact of striking prey during an attack.
Daspletosaurus horneri likely possessed integumentary sensory organs used for touch, jaw movement modulation, temperature sensing, and prey detection.
Evidence suggests D. horneri possessed integumentary sensory organs, possibly used for touch, precise jaw movements, temperature sensing, and prey detection.
Healed bite marks on a Daspletosaurus skull indicate the animal survived an attack.
Researchers hypothesize that low mortality among juvenile Daspletosaurus over a certain size was due to a lack of predation, similar to modern large mammals like elephants.
Tooth marks on a Saurornitholestes dentary suggest it was bitten by a young Daspletosaurus.
A juvenile Daspletosaurus specimen from Dinosaur Provincial Park shows bite marks on its face inflicted by another tyrannosaurid.
Daspletosaurus is classified in the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae within the family Tyrannosauridae.
The Oldman Formation, where Daspletosaurus fossils were found, was deposited during the middle Campanian stage from about 79.5 to 77 million years ago.
All known Daspletosaurus fossils date to the middle to late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, between 78 and 74.4 million years ago.
Daspletosaurus lived in North America during the Campanian stage of the late Cretaceous, approximately 77 to 74 million years ago.
Research on a large specimen in 2025 suggested that the distinction between D. wilsoni and D. torosus may be invalid.
In 2024, researchers suggested that Dinosaur Park specimens likely belong to the species D. wilsoni.
Gregory Paul proposed reassigning Daspletosaurus torosus to the genus Tyrannosaurus, but this classification is not widely accepted.
There is some evidence suggesting niche differentiation between Daspletosaurus and the coexisting tyrannosaurid Gorgosaurus.
Daspletosaurus coexisted with the tyrannosaurid Gorgosaurus in some areas, though there is evidence of ecological niche differentiation between them.
